<reason>Side A (CON) won a close, high-quality debate. A's case hung on the "missing middle" of informal fuel-dependent workers and the sequencing problem, and both threads survived the exchange. A's pressure questions were the sharpest of the round: Q1 exposed the tension between the motion's word "targeted" and B's "launch near-universal, tighten later" defense, and Q2 demanded a weak-registry country where compensation preceded the shock. B's A2 answer conceded that "compensation before the shock was never on the menu," which A quoted and built the decisive weighing around: certain shock, contingent relief. A also landed a damaging internal-contradiction point — the motorcycle-taxi driver is protected only while the program is near-universal and dropped once it "tightens" — which B's categorical-criteria answer never fully resolved. B's best route was the symmetry argument (subsidies detonate in abrupt uncompensated shocks, as in Nigeria and Iran), crystallized well in the closing, plus the unanswered regressivity/crowding-out arithmetic. But A's reinterpretation — that Nigeria's 2023 removal and Iran's hikes were governments executing the phase-out, not subsidies failing on their own — was more plausible and blunted B's examples. Both sides answered pressure honestly and directly with proper A1/A2 format; B was responsive throughout but was defending concessions while A was exploiting them. A made the debate easier to decide.</reason>
<best_rebuttal>A's Rebuttal 2: after B conceded "compensation before the shock was never on the menu," A fused that concession with B's own "tighten later" language to argue that the fisherman is caught only while the program is near-universal and released the moment it becomes targeted — converting B's capacity-building defense into evidence for the exclusion problem. B's symmetry counter (the subsidy's own exit is the harshest shock of all) was B's best moment but only partially neutralized the sequencing concession.</best_rebuttal>
